title: Ezekiel 15:1–8
context: The LORD speaks to the prophet, whom the LORD addresses as “Son of man,” with a short parable about the wood of the vine. Unlike other trees, vine wood is not useful for building or even for a peg, and once it has been burned at both ends it is good for nothing. The LORD then applies the picture: as he gives vine wood to the fire, so he will give the inhabitants of Jerusalem, because they have acted unfaithfully. Elsewhere Scripture pictures Israel as a vine the LORD planted (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21). Here the focus is not fruit but the worthlessness of the wood itself.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s word came to me.” Arminian readers note that Ezekiel presents the parable as a word given to him, not his own reflection, and that it continues the warnings to Jerusalem in the surrounding chapters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same formula and that the message carries the LORD's authority. The prophet receives and passes on what is given, which both traditions treat as shared ground about prophetic speech.

verses.text: “Son of man, what is the vine tree more than any tree, the vine branch which is among the trees of the forest?
verses.arminianNotes: “Son of man, what is the vine tree more than any tree.” Arminian readers see the LORD asking a question that exposes Jerusalem's assumption that being the LORD's vine made it more valuable than the nations around it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the vine was a familiar picture of Israel, as in Psalm 80:8, “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” The question turns that privileged image into a sober warning.

verses.text: Will wood be taken of it to make anything? Will men take a pin of it to hang any vessel on it?
verses.arminianNotes: “Will wood be taken of it to make anything?” Arminian readers see the point that vine wood has no use for building, not even “a pin of it to hang any vessel on it.” Its value lay only in bearing fruit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the parable deliberately leaves fruit aside. A vine that does not fulfill its purpose has nothing else to commend it, which sharpens the warning to Jerusalem.

verses.text: Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire has devoured both its ends, and the middle of it is burned. Is it profitable for any work?
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel.” Arminian readers see the image of a branch burned at both ends and charred in the middle, a picture of a people already damaged by earlier judgments.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the question “Is it profitable for any work?” Many readers connect the burned ends with earlier deportations from Jerusalem, though the text itself does not name events.

verses.text: Behold, when it was whole, it was suitable for no work. How much less, when the fire has devoured it, and it has been burned, will it yet be suitable for any work?”
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, when it was whole, it was suitable for no work.” Arminian readers see the argument from lesser to greater: if the wood was useless whole, how much less after the fire has devoured it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the logic removes any ground for boasting. Jerusalem's standing never rested on its own worth, a point both traditions treat as shared ground about grace.

verses.text: Therefore the Lord GOD says: “As the vine wood among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so I will give the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore the Lord GOD says.” Arminian readers see the LORD applying the parable directly: as vine wood is given to the fire, “so I will give the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” The judgment responds to their unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD speaks of himself as the one who gives the wood to the fire. They see his sovereign hand in the judgment, while the next verses state the people's own guilt.

verses.text: I will set my face against them. They will go out from the fire, but the fire will still devour them. Then you will know that I am the LORD, when I set my face against them.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will set my face against them.” Arminian readers see that escaping one fire will not save Jerusalem: “They will go out from the fire, but the fire will still devour them.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the refrain “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” In Ezekiel, judgment as well as mercy makes the LORD known. Both traditions see his self-revelation as the goal.

verses.text: I will make the land desolate, because they have acted unfaithfully,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will make the land desolate, because they have acted unfaithfully.” Arminian readers see judgment grounded in the people's covenant unfaithfulness, a real choice for which they are held responsible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same ground for judgment. They compare John 15:6, where a branch that does not remain is “thrown out” and burned; these notes name the image without merging the two passages.
